t: Buying dive gear and accessories without wasting money
p: Buying dive gear and accessories without wasting money
x: Some gear is worth every dollar. Some you can buy cheap. Here's how to tell the difference.

t: Start at your dive shop, and ask about price matching
p: Buying dive gear and accessories without wasting money
x: Shop prices can look high next to big online stores, but many dive shops will match the price of well-known online sellers. Ask. You get the same price plus a fitting, someone to call when something goes wrong, and service down the road. That matters most for anything you breathe from.

t: Never go cheap on life-support gear
p: Buying dive gear and accessories without wasting money
x: Regulator, BCD, dive computer and gauges: buy from a dive shop or authorized dealer, from makers with service networks. Have them serviced on the maker's schedule. Drysuit: fit and quality matter too much to save money here. See our wetsuit and drysuit guide . Never buy a used regulator unless it's serviced by a qualified technician before you dive it.

t: Where a budget option can be fine
p: Buying dive gear and accessories without wasting money
x: 3mm and 5mm wetsuits, if you don't dive often. Wetsuits compress and wear out over time anyway. A lower-priced suit from a big online store can be good value, as long as it fits snugly with no gaps. Stainless steel clips and double-ender bolt snaps. Cheap ones are often fine if they're solid stainless steel; marine-grade 316 holds up best. Avoid plated or "alloy" clips that rust, and very small clips that are hard to work with gloves on. Spares for your save-a-dive kit: mask and fin straps, O-rings, zip ties, mouthpieces.

t: Where cheap lets you down: retractors
p: Buying dive gear and accessories without wasting money
x: Gear retractors keep things like a light, camera or compass close to your body. Cheap ones often can't hold the weight they claim, so heavier items end up dangling, dragging or getting lost. For anything heavy, buy a heavy-duty retractor from a dive brand at your dive shop, with stainless steel hardware and a retraction force that's actually rated for your gear.

p: Buying dive gear and accessories without wasting money
x: I don't dive often enough to justify an expensive 3mm or 5mm wetsuit, so lower-cost wetsuits from Amazon have worked well for me. Stainless clips and double-enders from Temu have been fine. Cheap retractors were the exception. They didn't hold my heavier gear, even though they said they would, so I now buy heavy-duty retractors at the dive shop. My shop, Aquatic Adventures, price matches reasonable online sites, so I always ask.

t: Diving with a less experienced buddy
p: Diving with a less experienced buddy
x: One of the best things about diving is that new and experienced divers can enjoy the same dive. It just takes a plan built around the newer diver.

t: The rule that covers most of it
p: Diving with a less experienced buddy
x: Plan the dive around the less experienced diver: their training, their comfort, their air use. DAN advises buddies to set the pace, depth and time together and to plan for the slower or less experienced diver.

p: Diving with a less experienced buddy
x: Talk honestly. How many dives, how recently, where, and anything that makes them nervous. A diver with 100 dives ten years ago may be rusty. Agree on the plan: maximum depth (within the newer diver's training), how long, the route, and who leads. Set a turn pressure and an end pressure. Start back when either of you reaches the turn pressure, and plan to surface with a reserve, commonly 500 psi. Review hand signals, including "something's wrong," "low on air" and "end the dive." Agree on a lost-buddy plan. A common one: look for about a minute, then go up slowly and meet at the surface. Do a f

p: Diving with a less experienced buddy
x: Stay close, within easy reach. Check on each other often, not just air. The newer diver often uses air faster. Ask for their pressure more often than you think you need to. Keep it simple. A new site, cold water, low visibility and a deep plan all at once is too much for one dive. Anyone can call any dive, for any reason. When one buddy ends the dive, it's over for both.

p: Diving with a less experienced buddy
x: Say what you're comfortable with. A good buddy will plan around it. Don't follow anyone past your training or your comfort. Ending a dive early is never wrong. Want more practice? A Rescue Diver course is one of the best ways to become a better buddy. Checked November 27, 2026. p: Ear basics for divers: equalizing, when to stop, when to get help
x: DAN calls ear squeeze (middle-ear barotrauma) the most common pressure-related ear injury in diving, and most of it is preventable. Here are the basics, mostly from DAN (Divers Alert Network). This page is general information, not medical advice. If you have ear pain, hearing changes, ringing or dizziness after diving, see a doctor, and you can call DAN's medical information line (+1-919-684-2948, option 4, weekdays). In an emergency, call 911, then the DAN Emergency Hotline, +1-919-684-9111.

p: Ear basics for divers: equalizing, when to stop, when to get help
x: Start at the surface, before you go down, and keep equalizing gently every few feet, especially in the first 10 to 15 feet. Go down feet first, and use a descent line or the bottom slope to control your speed. Be gentle. Pinching your nose and blowing (the Valsalva maneuver) works for most people, but blowing hard can injure your inner ear. DAN describes other methods worth practicing, like swallowing or moving your jaw while pinching your nose.

p: Ear basics for divers: equalizing, when to stop, when to get help
x: DAN is clear: pain is not acceptable. If your ear hurts or won't clear, stop going down, go up a few feet until it eases, and try again gently. If it still won't clear, end the dive. Pushing through causes injury.

p: Ear basics for divers: equalizing, when to stop, when to get help
x: Don't dive with a cold or stuffy nose. Blocked tubes make equalizing hard and injury more likely. Don't wear regular earplugs for diving; they create an air space you can't equalize. Make sure your hood isn't so tight that it seals over your ears. If you get itchy, red ear canals after diving (swimmer's ear), DAN suggests rinsing your ears with clean fresh water at the end of the dive day. Ask your doctor before using decongestants or ear drops for diving.

t: If you think you've hurt your ear
p: Ear basics for divers: equalizing, when to stop, when to get help
x: Get out of the water and stay out until a doctor says your ear has healed. Don't dive again until you've been checked. Checked November 27, 2026. p: Diving Lake Allure, Quarryville, Pennsylvania: tickets, rules, depth
x: A small, private quarry lake in Lancaster County farm country, open to divers on weekends. Only 30 divers fit at once, so it's quiet, and it's about two and a quarter hours from DC.

p: Diving Lake Allure, Quarryville, Pennsylvania: tickets, rules, depth
x: Where: 140 North Church Street, Quarryville, PA 17566. Look for the dive flag by the road and turn in beside the old stone house. From DC: about 110 miles, roughly 2¼ hours by car from the White House. Traffic on I-95 can add a lot. Open: Saturdays and Sundays only. Gates open at 8 AM, and divers must be packed up by 4 PM. Season: the 2026 season opened April 11. Dive Peer pauses its monthly passes from December through March, so plan on spring to late fall and check before you drive. Run by: Dive Peer, which also runs Willow Springs in Lebanon County, PA. divepeer.com , 717-693-2440, DivePeer

t: Rules worth knowing before you go
p: Diving Lake Allure, Quarryville, Pennsylvania: tickets, rules, depth
x: Show your certification card. The only exception is students in an entry-level class with their instructor. Required gear for every diver: a BCD, a pressure gauge, a depth gauge and timer or a dive computer, and an alternate air source. No solo diving, ever, whatever your certification. Pass holders caught diving solo lose their pass. No swimming, snorkeling, wading or kayaking unless you're in a class. No spearguns, no fishing, no alcohol, no camping, no grills, and no jumping from the walls. No pets. Service animals and emotional support animals with a letter are welcome, on land only. Child

p: Diving Lake Hydra (the former Dutch Springs), Pennsylvania
x: The famous Dutch Springs quarry in Bethlehem, PA closed in 2021 and reopened in 2024 as Lake Hydra. The big change: it's now a training site, and you can't just show up and fun dive.

t: The one thing to know first
p: Diving Lake Hydra (the former Dutch Springs), Pennsylvania
x: Everyone in the water must be an insured, certified dive professional or be supervised by one. Lake Hydra is open to dive schools, organizations, and insured instructors and divemasters with their students. If you're a certified diver who just wants to dive, book through a dive shop or a guide service that runs trips there, then buy your entry ticket with the code they give you.

p: Diving Lake Hydra (the former Dutch Springs), Pennsylvania
x: Where: 4733 Hanoverville Road, Bethlehem, PA 18020. From DC: about 205 miles, roughly 3¾ hours by car from the White House, so plan on a long day or an overnight. Season: April through November. Opens at 8 AM. Tickets: online only, at least 24 hours ahead. No sales at the gate. Instructors with students and divemasters helping a class get in free. Depth: about 100 feet at the deepest. Air and nitrox: air and 32% nitrox fills on site. Buddies: required for everyone, including instructors. No solo diving. Contact: info@lakehydra.com, lakehydra.com

p: Diving Lake Hydra (the former Dutch Springs), Pennsylvania
x: Many of Dutch Springs' sunk attractions are still there, including a Sikorsky helicopter, a Cessna airplane and a boat called The Minnow, plus an old pump house. Look for koi and other freshwater fish.

p: Diving Lake Phoenix, Virginia: hours, prices, water temperature
x: A former rock quarry in Rawlings, Virginia, run as a scuba park and campground. It's where many DC-area divers do their Open Water dives, and it's open all year.

p: Diving Lake Phoenix, Virginia: hours, prices, water temperature
x: Where: 1 Quarry Lane, Rawlings, VA 23876, just off I-85 south of Petersburg. From DC: about 165 miles, roughly 3 hours by car from the White House. Traffic on I-95 can add a lot. Open: all year. Regular diving days are Thursday to Monday, plus Tuesday and Wednesday in summer. Winter hours are shorter, and some days need a reservation, so check the park's calendar before you drive. Shop hours: Mon to Thu 9 to 5, Fri 9 to 6, Sat 8 to 6, Sun 8 to 5. The lake closes one hour before the shop. Depth: about 60 feet at the deepest. The park doesn't publish a maximum depth. Who can dive: certified dive

p: Diving Lake Phoenix, Virginia: hours, prices, water temperature
x: In summer the top of the lake can be over 80°F, but deeper down you hit a thermocline, a sudden cold layer. The park says it sits around 44 to 58°F, so plan your wetsuit for the cold water, not the warm surface. In winter the water can drop below 50°F. The park posts current temperatures by depth on its home page. On November 18, 2026 it read about 63°F from the surface to 50 feet, with no thermocline.

p: Diving Lake Phoenix, Virginia: hours, prices, water temperature
x: The park has sunk a plane, a helicopter, vans, school buses and boats, plus training platforms. A large dive map by the docks shows where everything is; take a photo of it before your first dive. Look for bluegill, bass, turtles and crayfish.

p: Diving Lake Phoenix, Virginia: hours, prices, water temperature
x: Full gear rental on site, including 3mm and 7mm wetsuits, hoods, gloves, lights and compasses. Rental hours are shorter than shop hours, and late returns cost an extra day. Air and nitrox fills on site. Nitrox tanks must be labeled for oxygen service, and the shop won't fill some older aluminum tanks. Bring your own tank and you can fill it during the day; same-day refills must be in before 4 PM.

p: Diving Lake Phoenix, Virginia: hours, prices, water temperature
x: You can stay right at the lake: tent sites (with or without power), RV sites, cottages and rental RVs, plus a bath house and covered pavilions for gearing up. A "Camper Special" covers two diving days, two tent nights and unlimited air. Camping fees don't include admission. See the park's pricing page for current rates and the reservations page to book.

t: Good to know before you go
p: Diving Lake Phoenix, Virginia: hours, prices, water temperature
x: Fill out the park's waiver online before you arrive. Local dive clubs say first-time visitors each year watch a short orientation video. We couldn't confirm this on the park's own site. Fishing isn't allowed, and only electric golf carts and solar generators are allowed. Bring lunch and drinks. There's a small shop, but don't count on much food. Many DC-area dive shops run group days here, which is an easy way to find a buddy. Print our free shore dive emergency plan and fill it in for Lake Phoenix before your first visit.

p: Diving North Carolina wrecks from Morehead City and Beaufort
x: The waters off Morehead City and Beaufort are called the Graveyard of the Atlantic. Warm Gulf Stream water, World War II wrecks, and sand tiger sharks that hang around the wrecks. It's the closest big-ocean diving to DC.

p: Diving North Carolina wrecks from Morehead City and Beaufort
x: Most of the famous wrecks are deep, around 90 to 130 feet, and well offshore. That's deeper than Open Water training covers, and charter operators set requirements before they'll take you. One shop's listing for an offshore Olympus charter asks for: Advanced Open Water (or Deep) and nitrox certifications At least 25 logged dives At least 2 ocean dives to 70 feet or deeper, and 2 boat dives Age 15 or older Newer divers aren't shut out. Shallower inshore wrecks around 50 to 70 feet are a good first trip, and some shops run Advanced or Deep courses on these charters. Ask the operator what you qua

p: Diving North Carolina wrecks from Morehead City and Beaufort
x: U-352: a German submarine sunk in 1942, in about 115 feet of water. Papoose: a tanker lying upside down in about 120 feet, known for sand tiger sharks. Spar: a Coast Guard cutter in about 110 feet, a favorite for sand tigers and often the second dive after the U-352. Aeolus, Caribsea, Atlas and Schurz: other popular offshore wrecks. Shallower wrecks such as the Indra, Titan, Suloide and Hutton sit around 50 to 70 feet. Captains pick the sites the morning of the trip, based on weather and seas.

p: Diving North Carolina wrecks from Morehead City and Beaufort
x: Sand tigers look fierce, with rows of teeth showing, but they're calm around divers. They aren't fed; you see them living around the wrecks. Give them space and enjoy it. You can send profile photos of them to the Spot A Shark USA citizen science project.

p: Diving North Carolina wrecks from Morehead City and Beaufort
x: Summer water is usually in the 70s to about 80°F offshore, with visibility often 60 feet or more. Many divers still wear a 5mm wetsuit. Conditions change fast. Visibility can differ a lot between two nearby wrecks, and wind and swells cancel trips. Plan extra days. Boats leave early, often around 6 AM, and the run offshore can take two hours. Charters dive year-round. Summer is busiest; book early.

p: Diving North Carolina wrecks from Morehead City and Beaufort
x: Boats usually drop you on the wreck with a briefing and let you and your buddy dive your own plan. There often isn't a guide in the water, so you need to be comfortable on your own. Bring your own dive computer and a surface marker buoy (SMB); some charters require both. Nitrox is common, and some offshore charters require it. Save DAN's Emergency Hotline in your phone: +1-919-684-9111. DAN says to call local emergency services first, then DAN.

p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: The first year after your course is when good habits form, and when a lot of people quietly stop diving. These tips help you keep going and keep it fun.

p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Skills fade fast. Try to get a few easy dives in within a couple of months of your course, ideally with the shop where you trained. Fun dives, club trips and local quarry days all count. If it's been a while, take a refresher. Many shops suggest one if you haven't dived in about six months and have fewer than 20 dives. PADI calls theirs ReActivate ; other agencies have their own.

t: Make your first trip an easy one
p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Pick warm, calm, clear water with short boat rides. A group trip with your own dive shop is a great first choice. Tell the dive operator you're newly certified. They'll pair you well and pick suitable sites. Bring your certification card (or app) and your logbook. Operators may ask how many dives you have and when your last one was. See our trip reports for places other divers recommend.

t: Buy gear in the right order
p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: You don't need to buy everything at once. A common order: Mask, snorkel, fins and boots. Fit matters most here, and they're the cheapest to own. A dive computer. It goes everywhere with you, keeps your log and is the gear most divers buy next. See Technology Explained . An exposure suit that fits you, if you dive often in the same conditions. BCD and regulator last, once you know what kind of diving you'll do. Rent them until then, and have your own serviced on schedule once you buy. Want it on paper? Get the free first-gear buying order and packing checklist .

p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Your logbook is your proof of experience for trips and courses, and a record you'll enjoy later. Write down the site, your buddy, conditions, weight and what you saw. The DiveFolk Logbook puts your dive computer data and paper notes together in one file you can keep or move into a dive log app. Not sure which app? See Which dive log app?

t: Stay safe between dives and flights
p: New to diving? Tips for newly certified divers
x: Flying after diving. DAN recommends waiting at least 12 hours after a single no-decompression dive and at least 18 hours after several dives a day or several days of diving. Have a plan for emergencies. DAN membership includes a 24/7 emergency hotline and travel assistance. Dive accident insurance is a separate plan; check what you're covered for before you travel. Know your limits. Stay within your training and your computer's limits, and call a dive if something doesn't feel right. Anyone can call any dive.

t: Does your dive computer split one dive into two?
p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: How to stop it on Shearwater, Garmin, Suunto and Apple Watch, what Mares, Cressi and Aqualung do, and how to merge dives that are already split. You pop up for a minute to fix a mask, help a buddy clear their ears or check where the boat is, then go back down. Later, your log shows two dives instead of one. Your dive count is off, and neither piece shows the real dive.

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Every dive computer decides a dive is over after you've been at the surface for a set time. If that time is short, a quick trip up ends the dive, and going back down starts a new one. Many computers let you make that time longer.

t: How to stop it, by brand
p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Look for End Dive Delay in the computer's settings. Shearwater support told us the default is 1 minute and recommends 10 minutes if your dives are getting split. Shearwater Cloud can't merge dives that are already split; Shearwater says it is looking at adding merging to its Dive Shearwater app. Source: Shearwater support, October 2026.

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Garmin's Descent manuals list End Dive Delay under Dive Setup (hold MENU, then Dive Setup). It sets how long the watch waits after you surface before it ends and saves the dive. Choose a longer delay. We haven't found a way to merge split dives in Garmin Connect. Source: Descent Mk3 owner's manual, Dive Setup .

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Use Dive end time in Dive settings (scroll down from the pre-dive or surface screen). The default is 5 minutes and you can set 1 to 10. If you go back down before the time runs out, it's the same dive. Source: Suunto Ocean and Suunto Nautic dive settings.

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: When you come up shallower than about 5 meters, Oceanic+ asks whether you're finished and starts a 3-minute countdown. If you aren't done, start descending again and it returns to dive mode. Source: Oceanic+ FAQ .

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Mares' manuals for the Puck Pro, Smart and Nemo Wide describe a fixed 3-minute window: go back below about 4 feet within 3 minutes and the dive continues; after that, the computer closes the dive. We didn't find a setting to change it on these models, so a longer surface break will show as two dives. Check your own model's manual; newer Mares computers may differ. Source: Mares instruction manuals for the Puck Pro and Smart .

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: Cressi's manuals for computers such as the Leonardo say a dive started after at least 2 minutes at the surface counts as a new dive. That's a short window, so Cressi divers often see split dives. We didn't find a setting to change it. Source: Cressi manuals for the Leonardo and Raffaello .

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: The i330R needs a 10-minute surface interval before it logs a new dive. Go back down within 10 minutes and it's recorded as one dive, so splits are less common. There's no setting to change it. Source: Aqualung i330R owner's manual .

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: We're still checking these brands' official manuals before we publish exact steps. In the meantime, look in your manual for a setting called "dive end time," "end dive delay" or "end of dive." If you've found it on your computer, tell us and we'll add it here.

p: Dive computer splitting one dive into two? How to fix it
x: The DiveFolk Logbook joins them for you, for any brand. It suggests which pieces belong together using the time at the surface and, when your computer records it, your tank pressure. You can undo any join, then download a clean log. The free desktop program Subsurface can also merge selected dives. t: Steel vs aluminum tanks, and your weighting
p: Steel vs aluminum scuba tanks: how they change your weighting
x: Switch tanks and your weighting changes. Here's why, and how to get it right without guessing.

p: Steel vs aluminum scuba tanks: how they change your weighting
x: Steel tanks sink, full or empty. Aluminum tanks , like the common aluminum 80, start a little heavy and float by the end of the dive. So with a steel tank you usually need less lead on your belt or in your pockets. DAN puts it simply: steel tanks tend to sink whether full or empty, while aluminum tanks often start negative and turn positive as you use the air, so divers using steel need less lead.

p: Steel vs aluminum scuba tanks: how they change your weighting
x: Air has weight. An 80 cubic foot tank holds roughly 6 pounds of air, so every tank gets about that much lighter as you breathe it down. What differs is where each tank starts: A typical aluminum 80 is about 1.5 pounds heavy when full and about 3 to 4 pounds floaty when nearly empty. A typical steel tank is several pounds heavy when full and still a few pounds heavy when nearly empty. That floaty aluminum tank at the end of your dive is exactly when you need to hold your safety stop. Your lead has to cover it. Exact numbers vary by maker and model; check the spec sheet for your tank.

t: What it meant for one diver
p: Steel vs aluminum scuba tanks: how they change your weighting
x: DiveFolk's founder dives at Lake Phoenix in a 3mm wetsuit. With a steel 119 tank, 11 pounds of lead turned out to be too much, and 6 pounds was right. Your number will be different, which is why the weight check matters.

t: Do a weight check whenever something changes
p: Steel vs aluminum scuba tanks: how they change your weighting
x: New tank, new wetsuit, fresh water to salt water, or a long break: check your weighting on the first dive. A common way, taught in most courses: At the end of a dive, with about 500 psi left, stay at the surface with your BCD empty. Hold a normal breath. You should float with the water around eye level. When you breathe out, you should start to sink slowly. Too floaty? Add a pound or two. Sinking with a breath held? Take some off. Write the answer in your logbook with the tank and suit you used. p: Dive computers and dive tech explained in plain words
x: Your dive computer tracks your depth and time and uses a decompression model to estimate how much nitrogen your body has taken on. From that, it shows a few numbers that matter most: No-decompression limit (NDL). How many more minutes you can stay at your current depth and still ascend directly to the surface, with a safety stop. Ascent rate. Most computers warn you if you come up too fast. Slow ascents are one of the simplest safety habits. Safety stop. Many computers count down a stop near 15 feet at the end of a dive. Gas. If you dive nitrox, your computer needs the right oxygen percentage

p: Dive computers and dive tech explained in plain words
x: A quick trip to the surface can make your computer log one dive as two. Our guide explains why, shows the setting to change on Shearwater, Garmin, Suunto and Apple Watch, and how to fix dives that are already split. Read the split dives guide

p: Dive computers and dive tech explained in plain words
x: Many computers, including Shearwater and Garmin dive computers, use a decompression model called Bühlmann. Gradient factors are two percentages that make that model more or less conservative. GF high sets how close to the model's limit you can be when you reach the surface. For most recreational diving, this is the number that matters most. A lower GF high means shorter no-deco times and more margin. GF low mainly shapes deeper stops on dives that need decompression, so it rarely affects typical recreational dives. Settings like "low, medium, high" conservatism are usually preset gradient fact

p: Dive computers and dive tech explained in plain words
x: With air integration, a small transmitter screws into your regulator's first stage and sends your tank pressure wirelessly to your dive computer. The computer can then show your pressure, your gas use and an estimate of time remaining. The transmitter has to be paired with your computer and has its own battery. Signals can drop out briefly, especially when another diver's transmitter is close by. Many divers also keep an analog pressure gauge as a backup.

p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: You don't have to sign up for a full course to find out if you like breathing underwater. Here's how to try it, what learning involves, and how to pick a place to learn.

p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: Most dive shops offer a short try-dive. PADI calls it Discover Scuba Diving , and other training agencies have their own versions. You learn a few basic skills in water shallow enough to stand up in, then swim around with an instructor right next to you. It's a low-pressure way to find out whether you can clear your ears and whether you feel comfortable underwater. It's for ages 10 and up in the PADI version. It isn't a certification. You can only dive with a professional supervising you. If your try-dive includes an open water dive, the instructor may be able to count it toward a full course

p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: Before any scuba program you'll fill in a short diver medical questionnaire . It was written by diving doctors working with DAN and the Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society. If you answer "no" to everything, you're set. A "yes" doesn't mean you can't dive; it means a doctor needs to sign off first. Do that before your trip, not at the dock. See the questionnaire (PDF)

p: Thinking about scuba diving? How to try it first
x: The first full certification is usually called Open Water Diver . In the PADI version it has three parts: Knowledge: reading or online lessons with short quizzes. Many people do this at home before the pool. Pool sessions: practicing skills like clearing your mask and sharing air in calm, shallow water. Four open water dives: in a lake, quarry or the ocean, usually over two days. You'll need to swim 200 meters (or 300 with mask, fins and snorkel) and float for 10 minutes, with no time limit on the swim. Once certified, you can dive with a buddy to about 60 feet (18 meters). t: Wetsuit or drysuit for cold quarries?
p: Wetsuit or drysuit for cold quarries? Fit tips, including for bigger divers
x: Local quarries can be warm at the top and cold below the thermocline. Here's how to choose, and how to get a fit that works, including if you're bigger or taller than the size chart expects.

p: Wetsuit or drysuit for cold quarries? Fit tips, including for bigger divers
x: Choose your suit for the coldest water you'll reach, not the surface. At Lake Phoenix, for example, the park says the summer thermocline is around 44 to 58°F, even when the surface is over 80°F. 3mm wetsuit: warm water, or shallow summer quarry dives above the thermocline. 5mm to 7mm wetsuit, with hood and gloves: most quarry diving in spring, summer and fall if you go deep. Drysuit: water in the 50s and below, long dives, or if you get cold easily. Everyone runs differently. If you shiver, end the dive; cold makes you breathe harder and think slower.

p: Wetsuit or drysuit for cold quarries? Fit tips, including for bigger divers
x: Snug everywhere, like a second skin, with no gaps at the lower back, armpits or knees. Loose spots let cold water flush through. You can lift your arms over your head and squat without fighting the suit. The neck seals without choking you. Try it on in the shop, and move around in it.

p: Wetsuit or drysuit for cold quarries? Fit tips, including for bigger divers
x: A drysuit keeps you dry; the undergarment underneath keeps you warm. Try it on with the undergarment you'll wear. It should let you reach your tank valve and your fins, and kneel, without pulling. Take a drysuit course before you dive one. It handles differently, and many shops ask for drysuit training before they'll rent you one. Don't buy cheap here. A drysuit that leaks or fits badly is miserable and less safe.

p: Wetsuit or drysuit for cold quarries? Fit tips, including for bigger divers
x: Look for extended size lines. Many makers sell "tall," "short" and "plus" or "big" versions of their regular sizes. Check more than one brand's size chart. Cuts vary a lot; some brands run slimmer, others roomier. For drysuits, ask about made-to-measure. Several major makers offer it, using around 20 body measurements instead of 3 or 4. It costs more and takes extra weeks, so order well before your trip. If you order made-to-measure through a shop, it's fair to confirm with the maker that you got a custom cut. Checked November 27, 2026. Sources: Lake Phoenix ; DUI sizing ; BARE made to measure
